source: Search sweep for gap 1 (this session): paper-index and arXiv listing searches for 'secretary problem' with LLMs
finding: About 20 query variants (secretary problem, optimal stopping, sequential search, house selling, price search, with LLMs or language models) found no study that gives the classic or cardinal secretary problem to language models and compares them with people. The only 'secretary problem' hits were algorithm theory. Closest items are agent-stopping studies (d02, d05, d14) and LLM-vs-human choice studies on other tasks.
numbers: 0 relevant hits across about 20 queries; hits were learning-augmented algorithm theory (2103.02014, 2207.06272, 2307.06210).
limits: Absence of evidence. Google Scholar, Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex and the arXiv API were all rate limited and the WebSearch quota was spent, so non-arXiv venues were not covered.
agent_relevance: Do not claim LLMs stop too early on secretary tasks; it is untested. A probe of our own (cardinal secretary task with a known optimum) would be new evidence.

source: Zhang, Wan, Yu, Wu, Zhou, Tsang, An (2026) Judged Useless, Queried Anyway: Tool-Using Agents Rarely Turn Their Own Evidence Judgments into Stopping Decisions
finding: Seven agents (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-32B, Claude Haiku 4.5, Claude Sonnet 5 and others) were run in a retrieval environment where the search tool silently fails. They label the failing results useless 97-100% of the time, yet almost never stop on that judgment and keep searching until the budget ends. This is stopping too LATE on a failing source, the opposite of the human 'stop too soon' pattern.
numbers: After 5 consecutive self-judged-useless results, unaided Qwen3-8B answers on 1 of 292 questions; the other models in Fig 1 answer on at most 7%. Forced to answer at that point, Claude Haiku 4.5 is right on 114 of 284 questions, versus 1 when left alone. Answering there succeeds 15-17% vs at most 7% for continuing (7-8B models). A pre-registered replication on 300 fresh questions confirms the pattern.
quote: Prompt cues change when they stop but not what they stop on.
limits: Retrieval QA (HotpotQA-style) with controlled source failure; budgets of 8 and 16 actions. Some analyses are marked exploratory by the authors. Preprint.
agent_relevance: A self-reported 'this is not helping' signal is not a stop rule. The scaffold's stop test (G11/S6) should be enforced by the harness, not left to the model's own judgment.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) Judged Useless, Queried Anyway: budget, stated rule, call cost and enforced-integration conditions
finding: Evidence for gaps 5 and 7. A stated budget moves the 7-8B models' stops to the deadline: they answer at the last allowed action and move it when the budget doubles. A stopping rule written in the prompt is followed only partly, and a stated per-call cost is mostly ignored. Showing the agent its running count of useless judgments did not make it stop on that count. A harness-enforced rule (answer after 5 useless results in a row) works: it raises mean success for 4 open models and Claude Haiku 4.5 by +0.026 to +0.097 (Holm-significant), keeps the stop point fixed when the budget doubles, and is non-inferior in 18 of 20 tests where the source recovers.
numbers: Budget doubled: budget-cued agents move their answer from action 8 to action 16 and roughly double their tool calls on a failing source with no success gain. Rule in words: only Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen3-32B follow it, partly (hazard slope +0.09 and +0.08 vs +0.37 and +0.33 when enforced). Rule plus deadline combined: non-inferior to both parts in 14 of 14 pre-registered tests, and beats the rule alone by +0.138 for Qwen2.5-7B. A cheap lexical detector (few shared content words means useless) does about as well as the agent's own judgment.
limits: A visible budget acts as a deadline cue here, not as an evidence cue. No test of a threshold that falls smoothly with remaining budget as in humans (Baumann, Christian).
agent_relevance: A visible budget shifts WHEN the agent stops but not WHAT it stops on. Use a budget plus a harness rule on evidence; the data show they cover different failures.

source: Lin, Wang et al. (2026) BAGEN: Are LLM Agents Budget-Aware?
finding: Five frontier agents on four environments (Sokoban, Search-R1, Warehouse, SWE-bench) were asked mid-run to bound the remaining budget. All twenty model-environment pairs underestimate the remaining cost more often than they overestimate it, so they are over-optimistic and keep spending on tasks unlikely to succeed. Task skill and budget skill are only weakly linked. Acting on an 'impossible' signal saves tokens at small cost.
numbers: Correlation of task success with interval hit rate about r=0.35. Search-R1: Opus task success 75.8% but Sonnet gives better intervals (36.5% vs 23.1%). Interval coverage: base 10.5%, SFT 26-53%, SFT+RL capped at 47% (median midpoint error 28%). Early stop on 'impossible' saves 28-64% of tokens on failed rollouts and lowers overall success by 1.6 to 4.2 points. False-abort rate / saved failed-rollout tokens: GPT-5.2 Instant 6.6% / 64.1%; Gemini 3.1 Pro 2.8% / 55.7%; Claude Sonnet 4.6 3.3% / 49.6%; Qwen3-235B 4.9% / 38.8%; Claude Opus 4.7 2.2% / 28.2%. Savings near zero on Search-R1 (short rollouts).
limits: Predictions scored by rollout replay. Interval estimates are not the same as a stop decision under a budget counter. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Models do not know how much budget they need. Treat any self-estimate of remaining cost as biased low (gaps 5 and 6) and plan stops from an external estimate.

source: Agentic Abstention authors (2026) Agentic Abstention: Do Agents Know When to Stop Instead of Act?
finding: 13 LLM-as-agent systems and 2 scaffolds on more than 28,000 tasks (web shopping, terminal, QA) where the task becomes unachievable only after interaction. The main failure is TIMING: some agents never abstain, others abstain after many wasted turns. Bigger models abstain eventually but not earlier; reasoning mode improves timely abstention but lowers overall abstention recall. CONVOLVE, a playbook of stopping rules distilled from only 20 trajectories with no weight updates, raises timely recall.
numbers: Best WebShop agent: timely recall (AbsRec@1) 26.7%, overall recall 83.2% (Llama-3.3-70B). Best terminal config 21.6% timely. All tested models under 40% average timely recall. CONVOLVE (20 trajectories, 8 for validation): Llama-3.3-70B timely 26.7 to 57.4, overall 83.2 to 100.0, SPL 55.3 to 78.9; Llama-3.3-8B timely 6.9 to 12.9. Lessons written by the 8B model lift the 70B to 55.3 timely and 76.4 SPL. Plain in-context examples also help the 70B (55.1 timely, 97.0 overall, SPL 77.2) but hurt the 8B (overall recall 92.1 to 81.1).
limits: One training size (20 trajectories); no curve over number of episodes, so 'after how many' is only bracketed. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 partly answered: written stopping lessons from about 20 prior runs raise timely stops without training, and a small model's lessons transfer to a larger one. A short stop-playbook slot in the scaffold's memory is supported.

source: Xie, Wang, Mallick, Sun, Noarov, Yu, Mallick, Dobriban (2026) Statistical Early Stopping for Reasoning Models
finding: Head-to-head of stop signals with a 5% false-stop target on well-posed questions. A hidden-state linear probe holds the level when calibration and test data are alike but its false-stop rate inflates under distribution shift. Keyword-based sequential tests (renewal and 'Maxwise') hold the level on all sets. DEER-confidence and entropy rules also show much higher false-stop rates on MiP and MMLU than the keyword rule. The keyword rules recover 82-85% of an oracle detector's power on math sets.
numbers: DeepSeek-14B probe false stop: 3.00% (GSM-MC), 4.39% (UMWP), 30.77% (MiP), 30.83% (MMLU); power up to 97.7%. Qwen3-14B probe false stop: 6.0%, 2.6%, 40.4%, 40.6%. Renewal and Maxwise on the same models: false stop 0.75-9.0% on every set, power 39-88%. A one-component PLS probe cuts false stops on MiP/MMLU to 7.7% and 2.3% for DeepSeek-14B.
limits: Task is stopping on ILL-POSED questions (abstain), not stopping on hard solvable ones. Not an equal-accuracy head-to-head on hard math. Preprint v3.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: a probe is reliable only inside its calibration distribution; a sequential test with a guaranteed false-stop level degrades more gracefully. Without hidden-state access, a keyword or answer-stability sequential test is the portable choice.

source: Reasoning-Failures probe authors (2026) Effectiveness of Hidden-State Probes for Localizing Reasoning Failures
finding: On 4B and 8B reasoning models, a calibrated correctness probe at a midpoint cutoff says an answer is wrong but not what kind of failure. On incorrect 8B traces it misses 81% of cases where one step made the trace unrecoverable and 47% of cases where another attempt would succeed. No single probe locates the failing step better than a rule based only on trace length; at 4B a trained step probe failed to beat the length rule in any of 10 runs.
numbers: 81% and 47% missed; 0 of 10 runs beat the length rule at 4B.
limits: Failure localization, not an early-exit benchmark; small models; abstract level plus introduction.
agent_relevance: Do not trust a hidden-state signal to decide between continue and restart; a simple length or budget rule is a strong baseline that probes must beat (gap 4).

source: Oh and Lee (2026) Adaptive Stopping of Streamed Reasoning for Language Model Agents (StreamStop)
finding: Closed-loop tests on WebShop and ScienceWorld with several reasoning models: a learned text-only stop head beats validation-selected fixed token budgets (Const-B, Const-M) in most comparisons and rivals Full thinking with fewer tokens. Entropy-stability (EAT-proxy) and answer-consistency (Dynasor-CoT) stops beat fixed budgets only in some settings, and their ranking changes across models.
numbers: WebShop with Qwen3.8-27B: 42% fewer reasoning tokens than Full thinking at similar success. Table 2, WebShop first model, mean+-SD over seeds: StreamStop(0.98) 40.3+-0.3% success at 2675 tokens per episode; Const-M(0.99) 35.0+-1.5% at 1519; EAT-proxy 35.3+-0.8% at 1799; Dynasor-CoT 34.5-39.0% at 1444-3348. Token use is not identical across rows, so the match is approximate.
limits: The stop head is model-specific and trained offline on successful episodes. Authors say higher success with shorter reasoning on WebShop-Nemotron may reflect overthinking.
agent_relevance: Adaptive beats a tuned fixed budget in agent loops by a few points, but the best signal depends on the model (gaps 2 and 4). Always tune a fixed-budget baseline.

source: CLEAR authors (2026) The Shadow Price of Reasoning: Economic Perspective on Optimal Budget Allocation for LLMs
finding: A clean equal-total-budget comparison of adaptive allocation against a uniform per-query token cap with Qwen2.5-Math-7B. Gains are large when the budget is scarce and nearly vanish when it is ample. It needs a per-query length predictor and the authors show robustness to predictor noise.
numbers: Accuracy (%) Uniform vs CLEAR(Lambert) at 256/512/1024/2048 tokens per query: Balanced 3.0/12.4/17.4/21.6 vs 14.6/16.4/18.8/22.8; Mostly-easy 9.0/33.8/45.6/49.0 vs 33.0/40.4/47.6/49.0; Mostly-hard 1.0/5.0/6.8/11.4 vs 6.2/6.8/8.2/12.8; U-shaped 4.4/18.4/25.4/27.2 vs 18.6/23.2/26.8/27.6. Oracle at 256 tokens (balanced): 19.0. Abstract: up to 3x global accuracy in scarce regimes.
limits: Synthetic traffic streams built from a 7B oracle pool; this is allocation across queries, not a stop inside one query.
agent_relevance: Adaptive allocation beats a flat cap by 11.6 points at 256 tokens but only +1.2 at 2048, so the stop rule matters most when compute is tight. This agrees with Kalayci's 'modest at a tuned N' (gap 2).

source: Small RL Controller, Large Language Model (2026) RL-Guided Adaptive Sampling for Test-Time Scaling
finding: An MDP-trained lightweight controller decides each round whether to sample more. On AIME24, AIME25 and HMMT25 with four models (Qwen3-0.6B, 1.7B, 4B and GPT-4.1-nano) it matches SC@32 and ASC accuracy within about 0.4 points while using far fewer samples. A different lab from Aggarwal (ASC) and Li (ESC).
numbers: Average accuracy and average samples, ASC vs RL-guided: Qwen3-0.6B 22.9% / 29.8 vs 23.0% / 19.9; Qwen3-1.7B 45.9% / 23.7 vs 46.3% / 13.0; Qwen3-4B 54.4% / 20.3 vs 54.6% / 10.9; GPT-4.1-nano 27.5% / 26.7 vs 27.7% / 17.4. SC@32 uses 32 samples at 23.0, 46.1, 54.8, 27.8%. So 33-46% fewer samples than ASC and 46-66% fewer than SC@32 at kept accuracy.
limits: Accuracy differences are within noise; samples counted, not tokens; controller trained in-domain. Table text is garbled in extraction, so averages come from the printed Avg. column.
agent_relevance: Independent evidence that a learned adaptive stop beats fixed SC@N and the ASC rule at equal accuracy, mostly by sampling fewer. The saving is in compute, not accuracy.

source: Noah's Ark Lab (2025) Optimal Self-Consistency for Efficient Reasoning with Large Language Models (Blend-ASC)
finding: Dynamic allocation across questions with a hyperparameter-free rule matches the error of SC at 64 or 128 samples with 4.8x fewer samples on average over 6 model-dataset pairs (GSM8K, MATH, MMLU, GPQA-Diamond). Fixed allocation with oracle knowledge of per-question difficulty gets 3.75x. ASC is strong at low sample counts but stalls at high counts.
numbers: Blend-ASC 4.8x fewer samples than vanilla SC; oracle fixed allocation 3.75x; advantage stable across temperatures 0.4-1.0 and batch sizes.
limits: Measured as samples needed to match SC error, using 100 pre-generated samples per question; no per-token cost; free-response math and multiple choice only.
agent_relevance: Adaptive allocation beats even an oracle-informed fixed allocation by about 1.3x (4.8/3.75). An independent lab confirms the Aggarwal 2023 direction with a theory-backed rule.

source: PETS authors (2026) PETS: A Principled Framework Towards Optimal Trajectory Allocation for Efficient Test-Time Self-Consistency
finding: Adaptive trajectory allocation, using crowdsourcing theory with reasoning traces as workers, beats uniform allocation. The target is agreement with the infinite-budget majority vote.
numbers: GPQA: perfect self-consistency while cutting the sampling budget by up to 75% (offline) and 55% (online) versus uniform allocation.
limits: Target is vote agreement, not task correctness; abstract and introduction read.
agent_relevance: Another independent confirmation of the saving, with the caveat that the goal is agreement with a large-budget vote.

source: Rebeschini et al. (2026) Knowing When to Quit: A Principled Framework for Dynamic Abstention in LLM Reasoning
finding: Frames mid-generation abstention as optimal stopping with a value function over the prefix. A value threshold is optimal and provably dominates any fixed-position abstention. With the threshold set as a quantile of estimated values, selective accuracy depends only on the RANKING of the value estimate, so any order-preserving miscalibration costs nothing. Calibration matters only if the abstain reward r is set directly.
numbers: OlympiadBench, Phi-3 at abstention rate 0.9: selective accuracy 0.64 vs 0.34 for the best input-processing baseline and 0.33 for the best fixed-position baseline. Qwen: 0.91 vs 0.69 and 0.75. Easy sets: 0.92 at rate 0.1 and 0.99 at 0.9. Threshold transfers with mean absolute error under 1.2 percentage points; accuracy degrades smoothly under additive Gaussian noise on the value.
limits: Needs hidden states to estimate the value. Authors say it is limited when hidden states do not encode correctness, and that calibration of r leaves room for improvement.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: use rank-quantile thresholds instead of absolute confidence cutoffs, so order-preserving miscalibration does not hurt. Regret appears only with order-corrupting noise.

source: Context Gathering Decision Process authors (2026) The Context Gathering Decision Process: A POMDP Framework for Agentic Search
finding: In agentic search over four harnesses and three QA domains, asking the LLM to judge its own stagnation fails in both directions. A programmatic exhaustion gate based on action overlap and lack of new facts halts unproductive search without hurting accuracy.
numbers: LLM prompted to be conservative: infinite loops, 159% more tokens than baseline. LLM prompted neutrally: premature stopping that cuts accuracy by 5.0%. Programmatic gate: up to 39% fewer tokens with no accuracy loss, accuracy up to +6.9% on SWE-QA-Pro (stateful agents). Belief-state change improves multi-hop reasoning by up to 11.4%. The gate slightly hurts when the agent has no accumulated-fact state.
limits: Heuristic gate, three domains, harness-specific; depends on a persistent belief state. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: in tool and retrieval agents a non-LLM stagnation rule beat LLM self-assessment of when to stop. Supports a programmatic stop rule with a persistent state record.

source: Calibrate-Then-Act authors (2026) Calibrate-Then-Act: Cost-Aware Exploration in LLM Agents
finding: Evidence for gaps 8 and 9. In a Pandora's-Box-style task (K=3 boxes, 100 examples, Qwen3-8B), a model choosing which box to open and when to stop rarely follows the optimal rule unless it is given the prior over box contents and the cost explicitly. With priors in the prompt and thinking on, it nearly matches the oracle.
numbers: Optimal-policy match rate: 11.0% (no thinking), 23.0% (thinking), 20.0% (priors, no thinking), 94.0% (priors plus thinking; average reward 0.625 vs oracle 0.649). QA with retrieval cost: never-retrieve reward 0.213, always-retrieve 0.244; prompted multi-turn agents retrieve 61-98% and score 0.283-0.293, CTA-prompted is best. Code task: RL reward 0.259, CTA-RL 0.268 (+3.5%).
limits: Small K, synthetic main task, one 8B model. The optimal rule is computed by the authors and is not called Weitzman's index in the paper.
agent_relevance: Giving explicit cost and prior numbers turned rule-following from 23% to 94%. A scaffold step 'write down the cost and a prior before choosing the next operator' has direct support. It does not show a Weitzman index beats an LLM's own operator choice in real tasks.

source: Belloni, Chen, Wei (2026) Online Pandora's Box for Contextual LLM Cascading, with Di Gioia (2026) Cognitive Friction, rechecked against the new studies
finding: Re-reading earlier records c21 and c10 against the new studies. The Weitzman reservation-index view of LLM cascades has proofs and simulation but no real-LLM operator-selection experiment in this sweep. Di Gioia's real-LLM test (EM 0.500 vs 0.817 for always-retrieve, N=60) is the only contrary real-LLM data point. The new CTA, exhaustion-gate and Judged-Useless studies suggest why: stop rules without explicit costs, priors or enforcement are not followed.
numbers: From c21: oracle queries 1.30-1.78 boxes per period in simulation. From c10: EM 0.500 vs 0.817, N=60.
limits: Synthesis line. Gap 9 stays open for real tasks.
agent_relevance: Weitzman's index is a sound way to rank operators by expected gain and cost, but it has no real-LLM validation. Treat it as a design heuristic and test it.

source: Own computation (this session) of the classic rank-only secretary rule, for gap 3
finding: Seale and Rapoport (1997) is paywalled (Crossref and Unpaywall report closed access and no abstract) and Gilbert and Mosteller (1966) could not be opened. Their exact human numbers therefore remain unobtained. The theory side was recomputed: the best cutoff and win probability for finite n, and what stopping early costs.
numbers: n=10: best skip 3, win prob 0.3987. n=20: skip 7, 0.3842. n=100: skip 37, 0.3710; stopping at 25% gives 0.3504 and at 50% gives 0.3491. n=1000: skip 368, 0.3682. Limit cutoff 0.368, win prob 0.3679. A 25% cutoff costs only about 2 points of win probability at n=100.
limits: Computed, not quoted from Gilbert and Mosteller. No human cutoff or win-rate figure from Seale and Rapoport is in this file.
agent_relevance: Stopping a little early is cheap. Damage in agents comes from stopping on a wrong signal, not from a slightly early cutoff.

source: Bearden (2006) and Goldstein et al. (2020), statements about Seale and Rapoport (1997), reread this session
finding: Bearden says Seale and Rapoport found that subjects ended their search earlier than the optimal cutoff and that related studies (Seale and Rapoport 2000; Zwick et al. 2003) found the same. Goldstein et al. say Seale and Rapoport used rank-only presentation, which prevents people learning the distribution, and found no learning.
numbers: No cutoff or win-rate figures appear in either source.
limits: Secondhand. Closes the direction part of gap 3 but not the figures.
agent_relevance: State the claim only as 'earlier than the optimal cutoff'; do not quote a percentage.

source: Thinking Past the Answer authors (2026) Thinking Past the Answer: Evaluating Harmful Overthinking in Large Reasoning Models
finding: Defines reasoning sufficiency as the shortest prefix that first gives the correct answer. Stopping at that oracle point beats standard full reasoning, so models are limited by inability to stop. Practical early-stopping methods cut verbose overthinking but do not fix harmful overthinking, where more reasoning destabilizes an already correct trajectory.
numbers: Oracle stop at first correct prefix improves accuracy by up to 21% over standard reasoning; early stopping removes up to 50% of verbose overthinking.
limits: The oracle needs the answer; practical stops did not recover the gain. Abstract and introduction read.
agent_relevance: Upper bound for what a perfect stop signal could gain (gap 4), and a warning that cheap signals mostly save tokens rather than lift accuracy.

source: Pitfalls of verbalized confidence priors (2026) On the Pitfalls of Verbalized Confidence Priors for Calibrating Large Reasoning Models
finding: Off-the-shelf reasoning models put verbalized confidence on a few high values, and this persists through RL and limits calibration. A self-reported number is therefore a coarse stop signal; supervised reshaping (CalibSFT) is needed first.
numbers: Abstract level: confidence prior concentrated on a few high values, effect tested across 16 math and general benchmarks. Related c23: Llama-3.1-8B calibration error 0.044/0.104/0.050/0.015 by reasoning budget (none/light/medium/heavy).
limits: Calibration paper, not a stop-rule paper; abstract and introduction only.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: thresholds on a self-reported confidence have few distinct values, so a quantile threshold (d13) or a count-based vote margin is safer.

source: Replication search for gap 10 (this session): independent tests of OS-Pruner, OptPO and reliability-aware voting
finding: No paper was found that re-runs OS-Pruner (2607.11089), OptPO (2512.02882) or reliability-aware voting (2601.02970) on other models as a replication. What exists is convergent evidence from other labs for the broader claim that adaptive stopping on sampling saves samples: Blend-ASC (d11, 4.8x), RL-guided sampling (d10, 33-46% fewer than ASC), PETS (d12, 55-75% less budget). The exact OS-Pruner and OptPO figures stay single-source.
numbers: No direct replication found; 3 convergent independent studies of the adaptive-sampling idea.
limits: Search used paper-index queries only; citation-graph tools were rate limited.
agent_relevance: Trust the direction (adaptive stops on sampling save samples at kept accuracy), not the exact OS-Pruner or OptPO percentages.
